project_and_compatibility.implementation_language: TestCafe is implemented primarily in JavaScript with a substantial TypeScript portion and bundled TypeScript declarations. Tests can be authored in JavaScript or TypeScript and run on Node.js. Browser-side operations use TestCafe's Selector and TestController APIs. [S1][S3]
project_and_compatibility.node_and_typescript_compatibility: [uncertain] TestCafe 3.7.6 declares Node.js >=20.0.0, its repository tests the latest Node release, and the npm artifact was published with Node 26.4.0, so Node 24 and npm are within its supported range. TypeScript 6 is not verified: TestCafe bundles TypeScript 4.9.5, its documentation still describes TypeScript 4, and automatic compilation forces CommonJS, Node module resolution, and ES2016 target. A custom compiler path or manual precompilation can use the repository's TypeScript 6 dependency, but no source certifies TypeScript 6 compatibility and no project execution was performed. Use separate E2E configuration or JavaScript until a TypeScript 6 spike passes. [S1][S5][S19]
project_and_compatibility.operating_system_support: [uncertain] TestCafe documents Windows, macOS, and Linux support. Chrome/Chromium and Firefox can run locally and on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu, while native Safari requires macOS or a remote provider. The official 3.7.6 Docker image is Linux amd64 only and contains Chromium and Firefox. The Node package may work on Linux arm64 when compatible browsers and system libraries exist, but no current official architecture matrix or arm64 image was found. [S6][S11][S23]
project_and_compatibility.license_and_governance: TestCafe is MIT-licensed and owned and commercially stewarded by Developer Express Inc. Development and issue tracking are public in DevExpress/testcafe. DevExpress also sells TestCafe Studio, but the open-source runner does not require a commercial license or account. The governance model is company-led rather than foundation-governed. [S1][S3][S20]
project_and_compatibility.installation_model: Install locally with npm install --save-dev testcafe and run with npx testcafe; the official documentation also shows a global install. TestCafe does not bundle browser binaries, so Chrome/Chromium, Firefox, Edge, or Safari must be installed on the host. Video recording additionally requires FFmpeg. The official testcafe/testcafe:3.7.6 image is about 500 MB compressed, amd64-only, Alpine-based, and includes Chromium, Firefox, Node, npm, Xvfb, and fonts. Pin the npm lockfile and an image digest or host browser policy for deterministic CI. [S1][S9][S11][S23]
project_and_compatibility.candidate_scope_and_layer: Complete Node.js E2E framework with a self-contained CLI and programmatic runner, fixture/test DSL, selectors, assertions, waits, request hooks, API requests, concurrency, quarantine retries, screenshots, video, reporters, browser launching, and debugging tools. It is not merely a browser driver or a composed runner stack. [S7][S8][S9]
project_and_compatibility.authoring_and_async_model: Tests use native JavaScript or TypeScript async functions and await a framework-specific TestController chain such as await t.click(...).expect(...). Selectors are lazy query objects and assertions can re-evaluate them. Fixtures, tests, hooks, Roles, RequestHooks, and ClientFunctions form a TestCafe-specific DSL, but browser commands are promise-compatible rather than a hidden Cypress-style command queue. [S7][S13]
project_and_compatibility.build_pipeline_coupling: Black-box tests can target either the built Parcel application served by Gin or the Parcel development server through baseUrl. TestCafe does not require Vite, source instrumentation, or replacement of Parcel. Chromium native automation uses CDP without rewriting the application. Firefox, Safari, remote, and cloud execution disables native automation and uses the Hammerhead reverse proxy, which injects and rewrites client content at runtime but still does not alter the source build pipeline. [S6][S19]
project_and_compatibility.testability_instrumentation_required: No production build hook, special route, or test runtime is required for ordinary Chromium E2E tests. Stable IDs or data attributes are optional but advisable because TestCafe lacks first-class role/label locators. Proxy-mode browsers inject TestCafe scripts and may expose compatibility differences with strict security policies or modern client code. Deterministic PostgreSQL reset, fixture seeding, and server-side Yahoo Finance replacement require test harness or backend seams because those concerns are outside the browser runner. [S6][S8][S19]

Gaps included about ten months between 3.7.2 and 3.7.3 and about five months between 3.7.4 and 3.7.5. The repository was updated on 2026-08-20 by open Dependabot activity, but no later merged core change was found. Recent merged work was concentrated on dependency vulnerabilities, installation, CI maintenance, and releases rather than new E2E capabilities. [S3][S21]
maintenance_health.issue_health: [uncertain] GitHub reported 12 open issues and 4,864 closed issues on 2026-08-22, while the repository summary reported 36 open issues plus pull requests. Recent bug reports received some responses, but recent closures include stale-bot outcomes, and accepted issues can remain open for months. The small current queue is positive, but point-in-time samples do not establish median maintainer response, resolution time, or whether low issue volume reflects reduced usage. [S3][S21]
maintenance_health.roadmap_and_deprecation_risk: [uncertain] TestCafe is not deprecated and 3.7.6 was released in 2026. However, the public roadmap is materially stale: most entries were completed in 2021-2022 and the remaining planned items have no dates. The documentation release-notes index stops at 3.7.0 even though four later stable versions exist. The move from the Hammerhead proxy to native automation remains incomplete because only Chromium uses CDP; Firefox, Safari, mobile, remote, and cloud browsers still require proxy mode. maintenance_health.dependency_currency: [uncertain] Runtime support is mixed. Version 3.7.6 requires Node >=20 and the repository tests the latest Node, but it bundles TypeScript 4.9.5 and @types/node 20.14.5, pins a 2023-era devtools-protocol snapshot, and carries 97 direct runtime dependencies including multiple old major versions. Releases 3.7.5 and 3.7.6 addressed vulnerabilities and deterministic installs, but current Chrome/Edge 146 and WebSocket/CDP compatibility bugs were open in 2026. No complete dependency vulnerability scan or TypeScript 6 run was performed. [S1][S5][S21]
maintenance_health.wrapper_upstream_lag: [uncertain] TestCafe is not a WebDriver wrapper: it directly uses CDP for Chromium and its own Hammerhead proxy elsewhere. That avoids Selenium binding lag but makes browser compatibility the TestCafe team's responsibility. TestCafe 3.7.6 still pins devtools-protocol 0.0.1109433 and chrome-remote-interface 0.32.2, while open issues report failures with Chrome/Edge 146 and current WebSocket behavior. No systematic day-by-day browser release lag measurement was available. [S1][S6][S21]
maintenance_health.maintainer_concentration: [uncertain] DevExpress provides organizational backing, but current maintenance is concentrated. npm metadata lists one maintainer account, recent releases are published by Bayheck, and most substantive 2026 changes came from Bayheck and aleks-pro plus Dependabot and Copilot. The repository's historical contributor list is broad, but current review and release authority appears narrow. No staffing commitment, funding allocation, succession plan, or current maintainer roster was published. [S1][S2][S3][S21]

browser_and_runtime_coverage.browser_engines: TestCafe supports installed Chromium, Google Chrome, Chrome Canary, Chromium-based Edge, Opera, Firefox, and Safari. Chrome and Firefox support headless execution on Linux. Native Safari requires macOS or a remote/cloud environment. TestCafe does not ship a Linux WebKit browser and does not automate legacy Edge or Internet Explorer. Remote/mobile/cloud support requires proxy mode. [S6]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.browser_protocol: Chromium-based browsers use Chrome DevTools Protocol native automation by default. Firefox, Safari, remote, mobile, and cloud browsers disable native automation and use TestCafe's Hammerhead reverse proxy and injected client scripts to emulate and coordinate interactions; Firefox launch control can also use a Marionette port. TestCafe does not provide a W3C WebDriver or WebDriver BiDi execution path. This split creates browser-specific behavior and feature limitations. [S6]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.headless_and_headed_modes: Chrome/Chromium and Firefox can run headless with the :headless browser option and headed for local debugging. Screenshots and window resizing are supported in headless mode, subject to documented Chromium window-size quirks. Other installed browsers run headed unless their own provider supports a headless mode. Xvfb is included in the official Linux image. [S6][S11]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.browser_version_management: TestCafe detects and launches system-installed browsers or an explicitly supplied executable path. It does not download or pin browser versions. Deterministic CI therefore requires a pinned host image, browser package policy, or Docker digest. The official 3.7.6 container bundles Alpine repository versions of Chromium and Firefox at image-build time, but tag reuse and unpinned system packages should be avoided by pinning the observed image digest. [S6][S11][S23]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.parallel_browser_support: A single run can target multiple browser aliases. The concurrency factor launches N instances of every selected browser and distributes tests between them; a fixture can disable concurrency. There is no projects abstraction, worker fixture system, native shard index/total, or cross-job result merger. Browser matrices and CI shards require separate commands and explicit test partitioning. [S7]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.mobile_emulation: Chromium emulation can set a named device or width, height, device pixel ratio, orientation, touch, and user agent through browser options. TestCafe can connect remote mobile browsers through a URL/QR workflow or cloud provider, but native automation must be disabled. Desktop emulation is not a physical device, and cross-browser device controls are not unified. [S6]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.real_browser_fidelity: TestCafe uses installed vendor browsers, so Chromium CDP runs exercise real Chrome/Edge/Chromium binaries. Firefox and native Safari can also be actual installed browsers, but TestCafe's proxy rewrites page content and emulates events in those engines, reducing fidelity and introducing framework-specific behavior. There is no generic WebKit substitute on Ubuntu, and neither Chromium emulation nor a WebKit build would establish native Safari behavior. [S6]
browser_and_runtime_coverage.environment_determinism_controls: Core controls include an empty browser profile, window size, Chromium device emulation, request mocks, cookies, and geolocation responses through native-dialog handling. Browser flags and ClientFunctions can adjust some settings. There is no unified first-class API for clock freezing, timezone, locale, all permissions, seeded randomness, animation disabling, reduced motion, or cross-browser device profiles. These require browser flags, injected scripts/CSS, application fixtures, or custom helpers and may differ between CDP and proxy modes. [S6][S8][S13]

application_fit.dynamic_dom_synchronization: [uncertain] Lazy Selectors re-evaluate against the current DOM, actions wait for visible targets, and smart assertions retry selector properties, which should handle many HTMX swaps and asynchronous Handlebars renders when tests assert a post-swap state. However, selector snapshots can become stale, assertions do not inherently wait for an element to exist, XHR waits continue after timeout, and Chromium native automation ignores configured AJAX/page request timeouts. Retained DOM snapshots should be avoided and each swap should end with an exists/value assertion. No project spike verified these behaviors. [S6][S7][S19]
application_fit.routing_support: Navigo navigation can be exercised through real links, t.navigateTo, URL ClientFunctions, and direct fixture/base URLs. Each test can begin at a known deep link, while browser history can be invoked and asserted through ClientFunction code. Gin or Parcel must serve the SPA shell for direct routes. TestCafe has no dedicated waitForURL or back/forward assertion API, so route completion should be synchronized on location and route-specific DOM assertions rather than sleeps. [S13][S19]
application_fit.locator_model: Selectors support CSS, functions, text filtering, attributes, descendants, siblings, index selection, and custom DOM properties/methods. They are lazy and normally reacquire nodes after HTMX replacement. TestCafe has no core role, accessible-name, label, placeholder, or strict-locator API; a selector that matches multiple elements commonly resolves by index rather than failing for ambiguity. Prefer semantic IDs, visible text, explicit label relationships, or optional data-testid attributes, and avoid storing Selector snapshots across swaps. [S13]
application_fit.form_interaction: TestController actions cover click, typeText, selectText, pressKey, focus through interaction, file upload, drag, hover, and native-dialog handling. Blur can be produced with Tab or a click on another element. Chromium native automation fires browser-native protocol events; proxy browsers emulate events. This can test input masks, hidden-value synchronization, dynamic rows, and native validity, but tests must explicitly assert blur-driven state and use ClientFunction for properties not exposed through Selector snapshots. [S6][S13][S19]
application_fit.canvas_and_download_support: Chart.js can be checked semantically through ClientFunction or t.eval by reading chart data, canvas dimensions, or application state, with targeted element screenshots as secondary evidence. Core TestCafe captures screenshots but has no visual comparator. It also has no first-class download event, stream, suggested-filename, or saveAs API. RequestLogger can capture a download response body, while true browser downloads require configured browser preferences and Node filesystem polling/cleanup. [S8][S9][S19]
application_fit.network_and_api_access: t.request can seed and query REST fixtures. RequestLogger observes browser and t.request traffic, and RequestMock or custom RequestHook can match, log, mock, and modify HTTP requests/responses. WebSockets cannot be intercepted, and native CDP mode limits request mutation fields. Browser hooks cannot replace Yahoo Finance traffic initiated exclusively by the Go backend; that requires backend dependency injection, a fake upstream endpoint, proxy/DNS control, or seeded data. [S8][S19]
application_fit.same_origin_support: TestCafe can target the consolidated Gin production origin or Parcel on port 8000, where the repository proxy forwards /api to Gin on port 8080. baseUrl supports relative test pages and Roles. No application CORS change is needed for these topologies, although Firefox/Safari proxy mode introduces TestCafe's own reverse-proxy origin mechanics internally. [S8][S19]
application_fit.test_isolation: [uncertain] Tests return to their declared fixture/test page and TestCafe manages cookies and storage for Roles, while concurrency uses separate browser instances. It does not expose lightweight fresh browser contexts per test, and browser-process/profile reuse can retain state not explicitly cleared. PostgreSQL state is entirely external. Safe execution requires explicit cookies/storage cleanup where needed, unique portfolio data or a disposable database per worker, and concurrency disabled for shared mutable scenarios. Exact IndexedDB/cache/service-worker reset behavior was not empirically verified. [S7][S13][S19]
application_fit.external_server_model: Supported. Tests can use fixture.page, test.page, baseUrl, or environment-selected URLs to target independently started Parcel, Gin, Docker Compose, or remote deployments on arbitrary reachable ports. TestCafe does not require ownership of the application process. [S13][S19]
application_fit.application_lifecycle: TestCafe can execute one application command before the run and stop its child process afterward, using a fixed initialization delay. It does not provide declarative multi-service orchestration, URL readiness polling, Flyway state checks, or Docker Compose health integration. This repository therefore needs an outer script or run hook to build, start Compose, wait for PostgreSQL, Flyway, Gin, and Parcel readiness, then collect logs and tear down services reliably. [S13][S19]
application_fit.visual_regression_workflow: Core TestCafe provides page/element screenshots, full-page capture, failure capture, and configurable paths, but no baseline creation, pixel comparison, masking, threshold policy, review UI, or report merger. Search results for TestCafe visual-regression projects were predominantly small, stale, or archived. A project-owned image comparator could be built, but it must pin browser/image/fonts, disable animations, wait for Chart.js, maintain per-browser baselines, and upload diffs. Semantic chart assertions should remain primary. [S9][S17]
application_fit.accessibility_audit_integration: TestCafe can inject a current axe-core bundle through client scripts and execute it with ClientFunction/custom helpers. The README-listed axe-testcafe community helper was last pushed in 2020 and should not be adopted without a security and compatibility review. TestCafe lacks core role locators, accessibility-tree assertions, and ARIA snapshots. Open-source axe JSON can be attached to custom JSON/xUnit reporting, but this is custom integration work. [S16][S20]

reliability.waiting_model: Selectors wait for DOM presence; actions wait for a visible target; smart assertions retry Selector properties and ClientFunctions; redirects receive a fixed wait; and TestCafe waits for XHR/fetch up to the AJAX timeout before continuing. Important limitations are that smart assertions do not themselves wait for element existence, native automation ignores page/AJAX timeout settings, and an overlapped action target may cause TestCafe to interact with the topmost element after timeout instead of failing. HTMX tests should assert explicit post-action DOM/API state. [S6][S7]
reliability.flake_controls: Selector/assertion timeouts, explicit state assertions, request logging/mocking, fixture-level concurrency disabling, and Quarantine Mode are available. Quarantine reruns a failed test until it reaches a configurable success threshold or attempt limit; defaults are three successes within five attempts and it classifies alternating results as unstable. This is stronger than a blind retry but can multiply runtime and database side effects. No core repeat-each stress option, random seed control, or automatic per-test rollback exists. [S7]
reliability.isolation_model: The principal process isolation unit is a browser instance created by the run/concurrency setting, not a fresh browser context per test. Fixtures and hooks can reset browser and server state, and fixtures can disable concurrency for serial scenarios. Shared PostgreSQL state requires repository-owned cleanup or per-worker namespacing. Quarantine repeats execute the scenario multiple times, so fixture setup and cleanup must be idempotent. [S7][S19]
reliability.resource_usage: [uncertain] TestCafe itself has a 6.4 MB unpacked npm package and 97 direct runtime dependencies, but execution also consumes one full installed browser per browser/concurrency slot. The official 3.7.6 image is about 500 MB compressed; screenshots and FFmpeg video add disk and CPU cost. Proxy mode adds rewriting/injection overhead. No reproducible startup, runtime, CPU, memory, disk, or concurrency benchmark was run against this repository. [S1][S7][S9][S23]
reliability.parallelism_controls: Concurrency can be set globally to an exact browser-instance count and disabled for selected fixtures. Multiple target browsers multiply that count. For this shared PostgreSQL application, start at concurrency 1 or mark stateful fixtures disableConcurrency; increase only after assigning independent databases/schemas and unique test data. There is no native CI sharding algorithm, worker index fixture, or merged report pipeline, so future distribution requires explicit file/metadata partitions. [S7][S19]
reliability.flake_observability: Quarantine Mode labels stable versus unstable outcomes and artifact path patterns include the quarantine attempt. JSON/xUnit/custom reporters can retain per-attempt data, screenshots, and video. TestCafe has no integrated open-source historical flake database, quarantine registry, first-attempt trend dashboard, or replay trace. Long-term classification requires repository-owned report ingestion and artifact retention. [S7][S9][S14]

diagnostics_and_developer_experience.failure_artifacts: TestCafe can capture automatic failure screenshots, manual page/element screenshots, per-test or single-file MP4 video, test/report output, browser JavaScript errors, browser console messages through APIs, and selected HTTP data through RequestLogger. It does not produce a replayable execution trace, DOM timeline, HAR, or automatically correlated complete network/console archive. Remote browsers cannot use core screenshot/video capture, and local video requires FFmpeg. [S8][S9][S14]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.debugging_tools: Headed runs, t.debug breakpoints, browser developer tools, a Visual Selector Debugger with element picking, debug-on-fail, and Live Mode for automatic reruns are available. The tools can inspect current DOM and selector matches but do not provide time travel, trace replay, or a maintained first-party VS Code testing experience comparable to newer frameworks. [S13][S14]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.test_generation: Open-source TestCafe can experimentally replay Chrome Recorder user-flow JSON and the Visual Selector Debugger can generate selector expressions. It does not include a maintained core code recorder that generates complete tests. Visual recording, automatic selector generation, and an interactive editor are TestCafe Studio commercial features. Generated selectors or recordings still require assertions, deterministic fixtures, and maintenance review. [S12][S14][S20]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.reporters: The package includes spec, list, minimal, JSON, and xUnit reporters, supports multiple reporters, output files, custom reporter plugins, and output hooks. xUnit can feed GitHub-compatible test-report actions; JSON can support custom analytics. HTML, Allure, and GitHub annotation experiences require community reporters or custom processing, and there is no core shard-report merger. [S1][S14]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.documentation_quality: Broad but materially stale. Official guides cover selectors, waits, requests, browsers, concurrency, quarantine, artifacts, CI, Docker, and extension APIs. However, the install README still says Node 16 while 3.7.6 requires Node >=20, TypeScript guidance remains on version 4 while the repository uses TypeScript 6, release notes stop at 3.7.0, the roadmap is mostly 2021-2022 work, and the GitHub Actions guide recommends an archived action plus setup-node/checkout v1 and Node 8/10/12. Every current setup claim requires source/package verification. [S1][S5][S10][S12]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.local_workflow: Developers can run one file/glob, browser, metadata filter, concurrency level, or quarantine configuration from the CLI; headed mode, t.debug, debug-on-fail, and Live Mode support focused iteration. create-testcafe scaffolds a project. There is no open-source TestCafe UI runner, watch dashboard, trace viewer, or built-in last-failed/repeat-each workflow, so repeated failure reproduction needs filtering and a package/script loop. [S7][S13][S14]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.failure_log_correlation: TestCafe reporters can timestamp test results, RequestLogger can retain selected browser/API requests, and screenshots/videos can encode test/browser/attempt names. It does not ingest Gin, PostgreSQL, Flyway, or Docker Compose logs or build a shared event timeline. CI must assign a run identifier, use UTC timestamps, save browser console/request evidence, collect compose ps/logs and Flyway output, and upload all files in an always-running artifact step. [S8][S9][S19]
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.artifact_data_exposure: Screenshots, MP4 video, request/response bodies and headers, browser console messages, JSON/xUnit reports, and downloaded files can expose portfolio data, credentials, cookies, tokens, and external API data. TestCafe offers selective RequestLogger body/header capture and artifact path controls but no universal redaction layer. Use synthetic data, avoid logging secrets, sanitize custom reporters/hooks, restrict GitHub artifact access and retention, and do not persist browser profiles or raw sensitive payloads. [S8][S9]

github_actions_fit.official_ci_support: Weak. TestCafe has an official GitHub Actions guide, but it directs users to DevExpress/testcafe-action, whose repository is archived and explicitly says the team no longer maintains it. The guide itself uses obsolete checkout/setup-node v1 and Node 8/10/12 examples. A viable workflow should instead use current actions/checkout and actions/setup-node, npm ci, installed Ubuntu browsers, and npx testcafe. The official Docker image remains current at 3.7.6. [S10][S11][S23]
github_actions_fit.browser_caching: TestCafe does not download managed browser binaries, so cache npm through setup-node and rely on GitHub runner browsers or a pinned Docker image. Host browser versions change with runner images and are not controlled by npm caching. Pulling testcafe/testcafe can use the runner's Docker layer cache, but image reproducibility requires a version and digest; the observed image is about 500 MB. [S6][S11][S23]
github_actions_fit.artifact_integration: Use actions/upload-artifact under always() for screenshots, MP4 videos, JSON/xUnit output, custom request/console logs, downloads when safe, and Compose/Flyway/backend logs. TestCafe writes artifacts to configurable paths but does not upload, redact, annotate, or merge them. xUnit annotations and HTML conversion need separate maintained actions/tools. [S9][S14]
github_actions_fit.sharding_and_matrix_support: GitHub matrices can run separate browsers or manually assigned file/metadata groups, while TestCafe concurrency parallelizes within a job. There is no native shard i/n switch, deterministic balancing, worker-index fixture, blob format, or cross-job HTML merge. Database-mutating matrices require independent PostgreSQL instances or must stay serial. Quarantine attempts happen inside one invocation and should not be confused with GitHub job retries. [S7][S10]
github_actions_fit.container_compatibility: The simplest topology is TestCafe on the Ubuntu host with this repository's Gin/PostgreSQL/Flyway services in Docker Compose and published localhost ports. The official amd64 TestCafe image includes Chromium/Firefox and Xvfb, but a containerized browser must reach the application by service name, host gateway, or host networking; localhost points to the browser container. Official guidance uses --net=host for some cases and warns that it weakens isolation. [S11][S19][S23]
github_actions_fit.failure_cleanup: TestCafe normally closes launched browsers and can terminate an appCommand child process, but Docker Compose, PostgreSQL volumes, Flyway state, and independent Parcel/Gin processes remain external. The workflow should collect artifacts and service logs, then run docker compose down --volumes --remove-orphans under always(), with job timeouts and unique Compose project names. Cancellation may bypass TestCafe hooks, so disposable resources and idempotent pre-run cleanup are required. [S10][S19]

cost_and_risk.open_source_completeness: The MIT core supplies the runner, installed-browser automation, selectors, assertions, waits, HTTP/API controls, concurrency, quarantine, screenshots, video, JSON/xUnit reporting, and debugging needed for a basic local and CI suite. No paid service is mandatory. Modern visual regression, maintained accessibility integration, trace replay, CI sharding/merge, and application/database lifecycle are not complete first-party open-source capabilities and require custom or third-party tooling. [S8][S9][S14][S16][S17]
cost_and_risk.optional_cloud_dependency: BrowserStack, Sauce Labs, LambdaTest, and other grids are optional for hosted browsers and physical devices. TestCafe Studio is an optional paid IDE/recorder; open-source TestCafe can run compatible Studio tests in CI. Core execution, screenshots, video, quarantine, requests, and reporters need no cloud account. Local alternatives exist for most requirements, but not as an integrated trace/dashboard product. [S6][S20]
cost_and_risk.migration_cost: Moderate. JavaScript/TypeScript, async/await, CSS selectors, page objects, REST fixtures, and test data are portable concepts. TestCafe fixture/test globals, TestController chains, Selector filters/snapshots, Roles, ClientFunctions, RequestHooks, quarantine semantics, reporter APIs, and configuration are framework-specific and require rewrites. Keeping domain fixtures and database helpers independent from TestCafe lowers future migration cost. [S7][S8][S13]
cost_and_risk.security_and_supply_chain: [uncertain] Positive signals are the MIT source, public releases, npm integrity/signature metadata, SLSA provenance, and publication by GitHub Actions as a trusted OIDC publisher. Version 3.7.5 performed several vulnerability fixes and deterministic-install work. Risks are 97 direct runtime dependencies, browser/process/filesystem privileges, proxy injection, an official 500 MB Alpine image, and multiple old pinned libraries. No complete npm audit, image scan, SBOM review, provenance-chain review, or license scan was performed. Pin lockfiles and image digests, scan dependencies/images, restrict CI credentials/egress, and review request hooks. [S1][S2][S11][S23]
cost_and_risk.custom_harness_burden: High for this application. TestCafe supplies browser lifecycle, selectors, waits, HTTP hooks, API calls, concurrency, retries, and artifacts, but the repository must build and start Compose, poll PostgreSQL/Flyway/Gin/Parcel readiness, reset or namespace database data, replace server-side Yahoo Finance, handle downloads, integrate current axe-core and visual comparison, collect backend logs, split/merge CI work, redact artifacts, and guarantee teardown. Stale official CI guidance adds maintenance burden. [S8][S10][S19]
cost_and_risk.capability_delivery_tier: Core OSS: runner, JavaScript/TypeScript DSL, installed Chrome/Edge/Firefox/Safari support, Chromium CDP, proxy fallback, selectors, waits, API requests, request hooks/mocks, concurrency, quarantine, screenshots, video, JSON/xUnit, debug tools, and Live Mode. Official OSS companion: amd64 Docker image. Deprecated official companion: archived GitHub Action. Stale/community: axe-testcafe, visual comparison, richer HTML/Allure reporters, IDE and Cucumber plugins. Custom repository code: Compose/Flyway/PostgreSQL lifecycle, backend Yahoo replacement, downloads, deterministic environment, visual/accessibility maintenance, sharding/merge, log correlation, and artifact policy. Paid optional: TestCafe Studio and external browser clouds. [S10][S11][S14][S16][S17][S20]
cost_and_risk.ai_execution_boundary: Normal TestCafe tests, assertions, selectors, request hooks, quarantine runs, and CI execution require no LLM, model credential, AI egress, or per-run AI cost. Visual Selector Debugger and Chrome user-flow replay are non-LLM aids. Keep any third-party AI authoring outside required CI, provide synthetic data and least-privilege access, and commit reviewed JavaScript/TypeScript tests that run fully without AI. [S12][S14]

evidence_and_decision.confidence: High confidence in package version, Node engine, bundled TypeScript version, license, release history, npm downloads, GitHub snapshot, official-action deprecation, Docker architecture/size, protocol split, and documented core APIs because these come from tagged source, registries, APIs, and first-party documentation. Medium confidence in application fit, ecosystem freshness, maintenance trajectory, and harness burden because they combine documented behavior with repository-specific reasoning. Low confidence in TypeScript 6 behavior, arm64 support, issue-response distributions, resource/flake performance, and complete application behavior because no project spike or benchmark was run.
evidence_and_decision.hard_gate_result: [uncertain] Overall: CONDITIONAL PASS for basic JavaScript/Chromium E2E execution, but FAILS the unqualified current-tooling gate. Pass: complete MIT runner; Node 24 range; npm; Linux/GitHub Ubuntu Chrome and Firefox; external base URL; black-box Parcel/Gin execution; HTMX-capable lazy selectors and assertions; form, API, request mock, screenshot/video, concurrency/quarantine, and no mandatory cloud. Conditional: TypeScript 6 requires a custom compiler/manual build and was not verified; Firefox/Safari use proxy mode; Safari is unavailable on Ubuntu; downloads, visual comparison, accessibility, database reset, Yahoo Finance replacement, lifecycle, sharding, and log correlation need custom code. Fail: the bundled compiler is TypeScript 4.9.5 rather than the repository's TypeScript 6, and the official GitHub Action is deprecated. [S1-S23]
evidence_and_decision.deal_breakers: For a new suite selected specifically for current maintenance and community adoption, the decisive risks are declining npm usage, slow feature cadence, stale roadmap/documentation, an archived official GitHub Action, TypeScript 4.9.5 bundled against this repository's TypeScript 6, and incomplete native automation outside Chromium. Exclude TestCafe if first-class TypeScript 6, Linux WebKit, native cross-engine protocols, per-test browser contexts, trace replay, maintained accessible locators, built-in visual comparison, or native CI sharding/report merge are mandatory. It remains serviceable for an existing stable TestCafe suite that does not need those capabilities. [S1-S18]
evidence_and_decision.project_fit_score: [uncertain] 56.4/100 provisional weighted score. Application fit 65/100 x 30% = 19.50: capable selectors/forms/HTTP but substantial custom lifecycle, database, download, accessibility, and visual work. Maintenance 42/100 x 20% = 8.40: recent release and security work, but slow features, stale TypeScript/protocol/docs, and concentrated activity. Reliability 62/100 x 15% = 9.30: automatic waits and quarantine, reduced by limited isolation and protocol split. Adoption 58/100 x 15% = 8.70: about 176k weekly downloads and 9.9k stars, but clear year-over-year decline and stale plugins. CI 45/100 x 10% = 4.50: current Docker image but deprecated action and no sharding/merge. Diagnostics 55/100 x 5% = 2.75: screenshots/video/debugger but no trace or modern UI runner. Cost and risk 65/100 x 5% = 3.25: MIT/no cloud requirement, offset by a large old dependency surface and high harness burden. The score remains uncertain until a common empirical spike is run. [S1-S23]
evidence_and_decision.recommendation: [uncertain] Excluded for a new Open Asset Allocator E2E framework selection. TestCafe can technically run a useful JavaScript Chromium/Firefox suite and still receives security/release maintenance, but the task prioritizes maintenance and community trajectory. Its declining downloads, limited current contributors, stale roadmap/docs, archived official action, bundled TypeScript 4.9.5, split CDP/proxy architecture, and missing modern isolation, trace, sharding, accessible locator, and visual features create more project-owned maintenance than stronger candidates. Retain only if an existing TestCafe suite already delivers value; do not choose it for this greenfield suite unless a spike overturns these findings. [S1-S23]
evidence_and_decision.empirical_project_spike_result: [uncertain] Not performed. No TestCafe dependency, configuration, browser run, or GitHub Actions job was added. A validating spike would need to run TestCafe 3.7.6 on Node 24 with the repository's TypeScript 6 custom compiler or precompiled JavaScript; start disposable Gin/PostgreSQL/Flyway and Parcel/production topologies; verify HTMX node replacement, Navigo direct links/history, blur/native validation, dynamic rows, Chart.js semantics, a real download, REST fixtures, backend Yahoo Finance replacement, database reset under quarantine/concurrency, Chrome and Firefox behavior, and a forced failure with screenshot, video, request/console, xUnit, backend, Flyway, and Compose artifacts plus guaranteed teardown.
